question: Does removing the probability-simplex constraint from attention let one head dynamically copy and delete information while reducing representational collapse?

key_findings.claim: Cog Attention derives signed weights from query-key scores, letting sign encode input-dependent copying versus deletion while the OV matrix performs refinement.
key_findings.evidence: A path-patching case study contrasts a Cog head with a softmax head whose static OV spectrum must implement deletion; the measured QK/weight correlation is low for the Cog head.

key_findings.claim: On synthetic counting/distinction tests, Cogformer final representations retain larger differences as context length grows, consistent with reduced over-squashing.
key_findings.evidence: The authors adapt the representational-collapse tests from prior theory and attribute the effect to signed paths, though the tasks are diagnostic rather than downstream long-context benchmarks.

key_findings.claim: Matched language models show higher average task accuracy at 141M, 600M and 1B scale, and signed attention modestly improves U-ViT FID on CIFAR-10 and COCO.
key_findings.evidence: Tables 1-3 report 44.35 versus 42.98 average at 141M, 47.97 versus 46.06 at 600M, 46.21 versus 45.52 at 1B, and FID improvements from 3.39 to 3.27 and 5.99 to 5.85.

key_findings.claim: Using Cog Attention in every layer harms convergence; retaining ordinary softmax in the first and last layers is necessary in the reported recipe.
key_findings.evidence: The all-Cog variant initially improves loss then stalls after roughly 2,500 steps, which the paper attributes to unstable early sign semantics and homogeneous signs in the final layer.

method.core_idea: Replace nonnegative normalized attention weights with a signed, input-dependent aggregation while keeping transformer parameter count and major training settings matched.
method.mechanism: Signed QK outputs can subtract values directly; mechanistic patching, collapse diagnostics, pretraining comparisons and diffusion-image experiments test expressivity and stability.
assumptions: Attention-weight signs admit a stable copy/delete interpretation.
Matched parameter count and tokens isolate the attention rule despite different optimization behavior.
Synthetic representation-distance tests predict useful long-context robustness.

techniques.role: Allows positive and negative dynamic aggregation weights.
Separates attention routing from static output-value operations.
Uses ordinary attention at the first and last layers to stabilize training.

evaluations.setting: 141M/600M/1B RedPajama language models and 44M U-ViT diffusion models.
evaluations.metric: Seven-task average accuracy, training loss, collapse diagnostics and FID.
evaluations.result: Cogformer improves averages and FID modestly; the all-layer variant converges worse.
evaluations.baseline: Softmax Transformer, Differential Attention and Centered Attention at 141M; softmax at larger scales.

limitations: Large-scale comparisons omit signed-attention competitors because of cost.
Task gains are modest and no uncertainty or equal-wall-clock analysis is reported.
The copy/delete interpretation is based on selected heads and OV summaries, not a causal census.
Softmax boundary layers weaken the claim that signed attention is a universal drop-in replacement.
failure_modes: Early random signs divert optimization and cause a training shortcut.
Unbounded signed sums can amplify activations or cancel useful context.
Average benchmark gains can conceal regressions such as SST-2 at 1B.
reusable_insights: Attention expressivity and trainability should be evaluated layer by layer.
A dynamic signed routing rule can move operations out of static OV matrices.
Representational-collapse diagnostics need downstream causal validation.
open_questions: Can initialization or normalization eliminate the need for softmax boundary layers?
Does Cog Attention improve retrieval, copying and long-context calibration at matched wall-clock cost?
Are signed heads more interpretable or merely redistribute cancellation?

competitive_landscape.title: Differential Transformer
competitive_landscape.difference: Differential Attention subtracts two softmax maps with learned scaling to cancel noise; Cog uses one signed rule and argues signs directly encode copy/delete operations.

competitive_landscape.title: Centered Self-Attention Layers
competitive_landscape.difference: Centered attention subtracts a length-dependent uniform term to shift row sums to zero; Cog makes signs content-dependent and benchmarks decoder language models.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers need glasses! Information over-squashing in language tasks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct theory and diagnostic basis for representational collapse.
competitive_landscape.difference: Barbero et al. prove and measure information loss in causal softmax transformers; the target proposes signed attention and reports improved versions of those diagnostics.

competitive_landscape.title: Theory, Analysis, and Best Practices for Sigmoid Self-Attention
competitive_landscape.difference: Sigmoid attention removes row competition but remains nonnegative and supplies hardware/stability analysis; Cog adds subtraction and a mechanistic signed-operation hypothesis.

novelty_assessment: Content-dependent negative weights and their proposed QK/OV division are distinct from differential and centered attention. Evidence supports modest matched-scale gains and a real convergence caveat, not yet broad superiority or a proven causal solution to over-squashing.
reviewer_notes: Read all 16 extracted pages, including path patching, collapse derivation, scale/token ablations, image experiments and attention maps. Primary arXiv/OpenReview competitors were checked on 2026-08-23.
